lesson.title: Undoing Operations: The Inverse Property
lesson.summary: Every number has a partner that cancels it out under addition or multiplication, and that partnership is the key to isolating variables when solving equations.
lesson.body:
Every number has a hidden partner that can undo what it does. When you add a number and then add its partner, you land back at zero. When you multiply a number by its partner, you land back at one. This partnership is called the inverse property, and it comes in two forms: the additive inverse, which undoes addition, and the multiplicative inverse, which undoes multiplication. Understanding inverses is the key that unlocks equation solving, because to isolate a variable you almost always apply an inverse operation to peel away everything surrounding it.

The additive inverse of a number a is written -a, and it satisfies a + (-a) = 0. For example, the additive inverse of 7 is -7, because 7 + (-7) = 0. The additive inverse of -12 is 12, because -12 + 12 = 0. Notice that zero is its own additive inverse, since 0 + 0 = 0. The number zero plays a special role here: it is called the additive identity, because adding it to any number leaves that number unchanged. The additive inverse is what you add to reach that identity.

The multiplicative inverse, also called the reciprocal, of a nonzero number a is written 1/a, and it satisfies a * (1/a) = 1. The multiplicative inverse of 5 is 1/5, because 5 * (1/5) = 1. The multiplicative inverse of 3/4 is 4/3, because (3/4)(4/3) = 12/12 = 1. Here, 1 is the multiplicative identity, the number that leaves any number unchanged under multiplication. Zero is the one number with no multiplicative inverse, since there is no number you can multiply by zero to get 1; division by zero is undefined.

Inverses become powerful tools inside equations. Consider solving x + 9 = 4. To isolate x, add the additive inverse of 9, which is -9, to both sides: x + 9 + (-9) = 4 + (-9), so x + 0 = -5, giving x = -5. Check the answer by substituting back: -5 + 9 = 4, which matches. Now consider (2/3)x = 8. Multiply both sides by the multiplicative inverse of 2/3, which is 3/2: (3/2)(2/3)x = 8(3/2), so 1x = 12, giving x = 12. Checking: (2/3)(12) = 24/3 = 8, confirming the solution.

A common misconception is confusing the additive inverse with the multiplicative inverse, but they behave very differently. The additive inverse of a positive number is negative, and vice versa: the additive inverse of 2/5 is -2/5. The multiplicative inverse of a positive number, though, stays positive: the multiplicative inverse of 2/5 is 5/2, not -5/2. Also, while every number, including zero, has an additive inverse, only nonzero numbers have a multiplicative inverse. When solving an equation, always ask which operation is attached to the variable, addition or multiplication, before deciding which inverse to apply.

The inverse property depends on having a well-defined set of numbers to work within, which is why it builds directly on the idea of Number itself. As you move on to integers and rational numbers, you will see that every integer has an additive inverse that is also an integer, but only nonzero rational numbers have multiplicative inverses that stay rational. Keeping track of which inverse undoes which operation, addition undone through the additive inverse, multiplication undone through the multiplicative inverse, will make solving equations feel like a reliable, repeatable process rather than a guessing game.
